newsitem.title: INDONESIA: USDA REPORT TO TAKE BACKSEAT TO U.S. WEATHER - TRADE.
newsitem.headline: USDA REPORT TO TAKE BACKSEAT TO U.S. WEATHER - TRADE.

text.p: A closely watched U.S. crop report due out later on Tuesday will probably take a backseat to the weather in key U.S. farm areas, Southeast Asian grain and oilseed traders said on Tuesday.
Dealers said the acreage and yield numbers in the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) crop report would set the tone for the market but was unlikely to hold surprises.
The focus of the market will be more on the weather over key farm areas in the U.S. which have been dictating grains and oilseed futures prices on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT).
A dealer in Indonesia said the USDA data would not get "the deserved attention" because it would be "overplayed by the weather".
"Suppose you didn't have the weather, people will be looking at the numbers. If the yield was higher or lower than expectations, you will see the market going up or down.
"Now, this will take the back seat, as everyone will be focusing on the weather," the trader said.

"The expectations are for a good beans and corn crop. If for instance, the USDA revises downwards the numbers but at the same time the weather outlook is brilliant, then nothing will happen," he added.
Another trader said the market has been gyrating up and down largely because of weather reports over U.S. farms.
"You have seen how the market has been. One day up, the other day down. This are the typical effects of a weather market," one trader said. "And you cannot speculate on the weather."
Dealers around the region expect the numbers for corn to dip while soybeans will probably be little changed.
"Most players have been coming up with numbers that are basically the same with the USDA for beans in July and slightly below USDA for corn," one said.
Traders said concerns over the region's weak currencies and the level of domestic stocks will have a stronger impact on buying intentions rather than the USDA report.
Malaysian dealers said they expected domestic demand for U.S. corn and wheat to remain stable in the near-term owing to the USDA's report of a mostly fair harvest for both grains.
Offtake of soymeal could, however, be higher as a slight shortage of the material was already being felt, traders said.

"We still have ample stocks of corn and wheat and looking at the USDA's report, it appears that supply for these will remain stable at the least," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur. "Likewise, I think the prices will also be stable."
The Malaysian market has seen a glut in corn supply since May due to overzealous buying by importers.

Dealers said last week there were about 80,000 to 100,000 tonnes of corn in Malaysia's central region this week, enough to last for about four to six weeks. Wheat was also sufficent, flour mill officials in the country said.
"We can go through August and September comfortably for the most part," a flour mill executive in northern Malaysia said.
In the Philippines, grain importers said they expected U.S. wheat output to rise near analysts' estimates of 2.476 billion bushels.
One factor casting a shadow over the region is the development of the El Nino weather phenomenon, which may cause drought in several countries around the region.

"If it falls below this level, then we are in for higher wheat prices due to prospects of lower wheat harvests in other producing countries partly due to the El Nino phenomenon," a senior trader said.
